title: Rate Limiting and Abuse Control
summary: Quotas on every door - because someone, somewhere, will loop your endpoint all night.
objective: Protect every endpoint with layered quotas: centralize throttling middleware, survive restarts and multiple instances, answer abusers with honest 429s, and rehearse an attack against your own API.

vocabulary.meaning: Enforcing a maximum rate of requests from one caller.
A budget of actions per window - per minute, hour or day.
The status code telling a client it exceeded its quota.
A response header saying when the caller may try again.
A throttling model where requests spend tokens that refill steadily.

concepts.name: Costs are asymmetric
concepts.explanation: A scripted loop costs its author pennies and can cost you real money, degraded service for everyone, or burned third-party quotas. Rate limits convert unlimited exposure into bounded exposure. They protect availability first, budgets second, feelings never.

concepts.name: Counters must outlive processes
concepts.explanation: In-memory counters reset on every deploy and disagree between instances. Real limits need shared state - the same shared-store lesson caching taught, applied to security. If restarting your server resets the attacker's budget, you have built an attack rehearsal mode.

explanations.title: Layered limits beat one big wall
explanations.body: Professional APIs stack limits: a generous global default per account, stricter caps on expensive endpoints (exports, searches), brutal caps on sensitive ones (password change, login retries - which Level 2 already gave you). Layering means abuse degrades gracefully instead of tripping one cliff for everyone.

explanations.title: Identity and spoofed headers
explanations.body: Whom do you limit? Logged-in users by account id; anonymous traffic by IP. But IPs arrive via proxy chains - blindly trusting a client-supplied forwarding header lets attackers rotate fake identities freely. Know which header your hosting platform actually sets, and trust only that one. This single detail separates decorative limits from real ones.

examples.title: The honest 429
examples.description: Over-limit callers receive 429 with a Retry-After header and the standard error envelope - not silence, not a hang, not a 500. Well-behaved clients back off automatically; badly-behaved ones are now easy to spot in logs by volume.

examples.title: Reading abuse in logs
examples.description: One account id appearing thousands of times per minute in access logs is not a power user - it is a script. Limits plus logs turn noise into named, blockable actors.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throttling only the routes the UI calls, leaving raw API paths wide open.
commonMistakes.fix: Limits attach at the router level covering EVERY route, with per-route overrides - not sprinkled on popular handlers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keying anonymous limits off a spoofable forwarded-for header.
commonMistakes.fix: Use the connection IP your platform provides; document which header is trusted and why.

agentGuidance: Demand the limit table before implementation: route x scope (per-account/per-IP) x cap x window x response behavior. One middleware owns enforcement; routes declare which row applies. Any limit logic living inside individual handlers should be treated as a review-blocking smell.

project.title: Throttle Wall
project.brief: Wrap the Private Ledger in layered rate limits: a default per-account quota everywhere, strict caps on sensitive operations, durable shared counters, honest 429 envelopes - then run an abuse drill against yourself and document what broke.
requirements: Default quota applies to every route via one middleware; overrides declared per route class
Sensitive operations (password change, export creation) carry tighter caps than reads
Counters live in shared/durable storage - limits survive a server restart
Over-limit responses: 429 status, standard error envelope, Retry-After header set
Abuse drill documented: a script hammers three endpoints; observed behavior and log evidence recorded

title: Database Indexing and Performance
summary: Making queries fast on purpose: indexes, query plans and the N+1 hunt.
objective: Diagnose slow queries with query plans instead of guesses, add indexes that match real query patterns, eliminate N+1 access patterns, and pay attention to the write-side cost indexes charge.

vocabulary.meaning: A lookup structure the database maintains so rows can be found without scanning everything.
The database's own explanation of how it will execute a query - scans, index uses, join orders.
Reading every row to answer a query - the slow path indexes help avoid.
An index over multiple columns, matching queries that filter them together in order.
One query for a list, then one more per item - a hidden multiplication of database round trips.

concepts.name: Measure first, optimize second
concepts.explanation: 'Feels slow' is not a diagnosis. The database will TELL you how it executes a query - ask with EXPLAIN (or your tool's equivalent). Plans turn performance work from superstition into observation: scan became index seek, rows examined dropped. Before and after, plans or it did not happen.

concepts.name: Indexes are a trade, not a gift
concepts.explanation: Every index speeds specific reads and taxes every write on the table - storage too. The skill is matching few, well-chosen indexes to your actual hot queries, discovered from logs and plans, not carpet-bombing every column on a hunch.

explanations.title: Matching the index to the question
explanations.body: A composite index serves queries filtering columns left-to-right: an index on (user_id, date) powers WHERE user_id = ? AND date > ?, partially serves user_id alone, and does nothing for date alone. Read your plan: if it shows a scan where you expected an index, either the index is missing or the query does not match its shape.

explanations.title: The N+1 pattern
explanations.body: Fetch fifty expenses, then ask the database for each owner's name separately: fifty-one queries where one join would do. ORMs make this easy to create and invisible until traffic grows. Detect it by counting queries per page render; fix it by fetching related data in the same query or an explicit batch.

examples.title: Plan before and after
examples.description: The ledger's list-by-month query scans the whole expenses table. EXPLAIN says Seq Scan, rows examined: all of them. Add composite index (user_id, date); the same plan now shows an index range scan examining only matching rows. Same code, different conversation with the database.

examples.title: Write tax made visible
examples.description: Insert one thousand synthetic expenses before and after adding an index and compare insert time. Slower now - that is the maintenance fee. Worth paying for hot reads; wasteful for columns nobody filters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding an index for every column 'to be safe'.
commonMistakes.fix: Index from evidence: hot queries from logs and plans first. Every extra index charges every insert, update and delete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Claiming a speedup without capturing plans or timings.
commonMistakes.fix: Before/after evidence or it did not happen - plans pasted, timings recorded honestly, including 'no meaningful difference' results.

agentGuidance: Standing rule for any performance task: 'Show me the query plan BEFORE changing anything, and again after. Include rows examined.' This keeps agents honest about optimization claims and teaches you the database's vocabulary simultaneously.

project.title: Query Clinic
project.brief: Run a performance clinic on the Ledger: capture plans, add one well-chosen composite index through a migration, eliminate an N+1 from the list endpoint, and document the whole investigation with before/after evidence.
requirements: Slowest realistic query identified from actual plans, not intuition - investigation notes included

architecture: Index choices documented against actual query patterns - no speculative indexes shipped
testing: Plans captured before AND after, pasted as evidence

Then seed ten times more rows than I did, re-run the target query, and report whether my fix still holds or merely moved the cliff.

title: Background Jobs and Queues
summary: Moving slow work out of the request path - workers, retries with backoff, and failures with a paper trail.
objective: Move slow work out of HTTP requests into queued background jobs processed by workers, with retries that back off, failures that land somewhere visible, and job states users can see.

vocabulary.meaning: A unit of work recorded to be done later, outside any waiting request.
The ordered holding area where pending jobs wait.
A separate process that picks up jobs and runs them.
Waiting progressively longer between retry attempts instead of hammering.
Where jobs go after exhausting retries - visible, not vanished.

concepts.name: Short requests, deferred work
concepts.explanation: Anything slower than a breath - emails, report generation, file processing, calling slow third parties - belongs in a job. The request's new responsibility shrinks to: validate, enqueue, respond fast with a way to check progress later. Users get snappy responses; slow work gets room to fail and retry safely.

concepts.name: Jobs WILL run twice someday
concepts.explanation: Workers crash mid-job, restart, and pick the job up again. Most queue systems promise at-least-once delivery - meaning duplicate execution is a design assumption, not bad luck. Handlers that would corrupt state when rerun need guards now; the deep dive arrives in Level 4's idempotency module, but the awareness starts here.

explanations.title: Anatomy of the pipeline
explanations.body: Request handler enqueues a job describing WORK TO DO (a payload), not doing it. A broker holds the queue - from a simple database table used as a queue to dedicated message brokers; start boring and local. A worker loop claims a job, runs it, records success, or records failure and reschedules with growing delays. After the final attempt, the job moves to dead-letter status where humans review it.

explanations.title: Visibility is half the system
explanations.body: Silent background work rots: nobody notices failures for weeks. Minimum viable observability: every job has a status (pending, running, done, failed, dead-letter), failed counts are glanceable, and each dead-letter job keeps its error and payload for diagnosis. Your L3 observability habits apply to queues from day one.

examples.title: Export without the spin
examples.description: Generating a large CSV inline risks timeouts and ties up workers handling web requests. Instead: POST /exports creates an export job and returns 202 with a status URL. User polls or refreshes; when done, the download link appears. Slow became invisible.

examples.title: Backoff in action
examples.description: A flaky external dependency fails the job. Attempt 1 immediate, attempt 2 after ~30 seconds, attempt 3 after ~2 minutes, then dead-letter. The pattern survives transient blips without amplifying an outage - the difference between resilient and robotic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sending email or generating reports inline in the request handler.
commonMistakes.fix: If any step could take seconds, enqueue it. Respond 202 + status endpoint. The request path owes users speed, not completion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Jobs failing silently - no statuses, no dead letters, just vanishing work.
commonMistakes.fix: Job states persisted and viewable; exhausted jobs land somewhere a human reviews. Invisible failure is worse than failure.

agentGuidance: Require a job contract table before any queue code: job name, payload fields, triggering action, max attempts, backoff curve, dead-letter policy. One worker loop processes all jobs through one runner so logging, retries and statuses stay uniform - per-job bespoke retry logic is how queues become haunted graveyards.

project.title: Job Bench
project.brief: Give the Ledger a real job system: CSV export and nightly summary generation move to background workers with retries, backoff, dead-letter review, and status endpoints - all observable, all restart-safe.
requirements: POST creating an export enqueues a job and responds quickly with a status reference - no inline generation
Worker processes jobs with persisted status transitions: pending, running, done, failed, dead-letter
Failed jobs retry with growing backoff, then land in dead-letter retaining error details and payload

Scheduled job produces the daily summary without any HTTP request triggering it
Queued jobs survive a worker restart - nothing lost, duplicates handled honestly

Two producers: export endpoint (202 + status URL) and a scheduler tick producing the daily summary. Persist statuses; expose GET /jobs/:id. Simulate a failing job type to exercise retries and dead-lettering end to end.

functional: Export request returns promptly with a status reference; artifact downloadable on completion
Simulated always-failing job retried per the contract, then dead-lettered with error preserved
Daily-summary job ran without any HTTP trigger - proof shown
Status endpoint reports accurate state for jobs in every state
architecture: Single worker loop and runner serve ALL job types - contract table maps names to handlers
Queue backed by durable storage; pending jobs survive process kill
security: Job payloads contain ids and parameters, not bulk sensitive data; dead-letter contents reviewed for secrets

verificationPrompt: Audit my Job Bench with suspicion about what happens when things go wrong - because in this system they are supposed to. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) interrupt a running job (kill the worker) - does the job recover without duplicating side effects? Report exactly what you observed, (2) force repeated failure - does backoff follow the documented contract and does the job land in dead-letter with usable diagnostics, (3) can user A read user B's job status through any endpoint manipulation, (4) do queued jobs genuinely survive restart? Then tell me: which job, if silently lost right now, would upset users most - and how long until anyone noticed?
reviewQuestions: Which operation did YOU move out of the request path, and how did users' experience change?
Why does at-least-once delivery mean your handlers must tolerate reruns?
Where do your dead letters go, and who looks at them?

title: Payments Integration
summary: Charging money safely: hosted checkout, verified webhooks, idempotent event handling and reconciliation.
objective: Integrate a hosted payment provider's test mode end to end: server-created checkouts, signature-verified webhooks that survive duplicate deliveries, amounts decided only by the server, and a reconciliation habit that catches what automation missed.

vocabulary.meaning: A service that handles card details and money movement so you never touch raw card numbers.
A server-created payment link the user completes on the provider's own pages.
The provider calling YOUR server to report real-world events like payments.
Cryptographically checking a webhook truly came from the provider, unmodified.
A unique request marker so retrying never performs an action twice.
Periodically comparing your records against the provider's records for drift.

concepts.name: Never touch card numbers
concepts.explanation: Card data has heavy compliance obligations you cannot shoulder as a beginner - or as most companies. Hosted checkout moves the sensitive collection onto the provider's pages; your system sees only references and outcomes. If code anywhere in your project could see a card number, the design is wrong.

concepts.name: The webhook is the source of truth
concepts.explanation: A success redirect is a rumor; the webhook is the fact. Browsers close, refreshes interrupt, but the provider's webhook arrives from their servers reporting what actually happened. Grant paid features ONLY on verified webhook evidence - never on client-side claims of success.

explanations.title: The money path, drawn honestly
explanations.body: User clicks upgrade; your SERVER creates a checkout session with amount and currency it computes itself - never trusting any amount sent from the browser. User pays on provider-hosted pages. Provider sends webhooks to your endpoint; each one is verified against its signature, recorded, and processed idempotently by recording processed event ids. Only then does the account flip to pro. Every arrow in this path is a place amateurs leak money.

explanations.title: Duplicates, retries and reconciliation
explanations.body: Providers deliver webhooks at-least-once: expect duplicates and process them harmlessly by remembering which event ids already applied. Server crashes between receiving and processing must also recover - recording before acting or acting atomically with recording. And because no pipeline is perfect, schedule reconciliation: periodically compare your pro accounts against the provider's subscription list and investigate every mismatch.

examples.title: The forged-webhook probe
examples.description: An attacker POSTs a fake 'payment succeeded' event to your webhook URL. Without signature verification this grants free pro access instantly. With verification, the forgery fails the signature check and gets a 400 plus a log entry. One middleware stands between you and free-product day.

examples.title: Test mode discipline
examples.description: Providers offer test modes with fake cards and separate test keys. Development happens entirely in test mode; keys live in environment variables - secret key server-side only. The moment a provider key appears in frontend code or git history, rotate it and treat the exposure as an incident.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting the browser redirect back from checkout to grant paid features.
commonMistakes.fix: Redirects are cosmetic. State changes ride on verified webhooks only. The client's 'success' page merely waits for the truth to arrive.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accepting amounts, currencies or product ids from the client at checkout creation.
commonMistakes.fix: The server owns the price book. Client says WHICH thing they want; server says what it costs.

agentGuidance: Before implementation, make your agent draw the complete money path as text: every hop where amount originates, every state transition, every place a duplicate delivery could strike. Ask where the secret key lives and prove it appears nowhere else. Payments are where 'the agent said it works' becomes genuinely dangerous - verify like it is your money.

project.title: Paywall Gate
project.brief: Add a Pro tier to the Ledger through a hosted provider's TEST mode: server-side checkout sessions, signature-verified idempotent webhooks flipping accounts to pro, one gated feature behind the paywall, and a documented reconciliation checklist.
requirements: Checkout session created server-side with price computed by the server; provider secret key from env, never committed
Webhook endpoint verifies signatures; forged or unsigned requests rejected with 400 and logged
Duplicate webhook deliveries produce exactly one account upgrade (processed-event ids recorded)
One feature gated: pro users get unlimited exports, free users hit the export quota
Events stored with type, id, timestamp and outcome - a queryable audit trail
Reconciliation checklist documented: what to compare monthly against the provider's dashboard
project.agentContext: Integrate a hosted payment provider's TEST mode into my Expense Ledger as a Pro tier. Flow: upgrade button calls my server, server creates checkout session using its own price config; webhook endpoint verifies signatures before anything else, stores every event, processes upgrades idempotently via processed-event-id records; export feature gated by tier. All keys from env vars - test-mode only. Draw me the full money path first including failure points, then implement. Include a manual refund/cancel rehearsal in test mode.

functional: Full purchase journey works in test mode: click, pay with test card, webhook flips account, gated feature unlocks
Forged webhook (valid JSON, no valid signature) rejected 400 without side effects
Same webhook replayed twice upgrades exactly once - second delivery is a logged no-op
Free-tier export hits quota wall; pro-tier export passes
architecture: Amount/currency originate exclusively in server-side config - provable by grep
Webhook processing records-before-or-atomic: crash between receive and apply recovers correctly
security: Provider secret exists only in env vars on the server; absent from repo history and all logs
Every webhook's signature verified before parsing proceeds
Audit trail answers: who became pro, when, via which event id
testing: Replay, forgery and happy-path scenarios scripted and passing against the real webhook endpoint
Refund/cancel path rehearsed in test mode with expected downgrade behavior observed
production: README documents the money-path diagram, env vars needed, and the reconciliation checklist

verificationPrompt: Conduct a hostile audit of my Paywall Gate - assume attackers get everything except my provider account and secret key. Attempt each and report PASS or FAIL against my DoD: (1) forge a payment-success webhook without a signature - did I get pro for free?, (2) replay a captured legitimate webhook multiple times - did I gain anything extra?, (3) tamper with checkout parameters client-side to name my own price - did the server honor my number?, (4) hunt my logs and repo for any trace of the secret key. Finally: trace one real test purchase end to end through every log line, and tell me where an auditor would still have questions.
reviewQuestions: Why is the success redirect untrustworthy while the webhook is authoritative?
Walk through how a duplicated webhook fails to double-upgrade anyone.
What does reconciliation catch that real-time processing missed?

Treat webhooks as untrusted input until signatures verify
Keep money-state changes idempotent, audited and reconciled

title: Observability Foundation
summary: Logs, metrics and traces that answer questions at 3am - plus alerts tied to what users actually feel.
objective: Instrument the Ledger so any incident can be diagnosed from evidence: structured logs with correlation ids, per-endpoint health metrics, a stated SLO with an alert rule, and an incident drill proving the tools work under fire.

vocabulary.meaning: Log lines written as queryable fields (JSON), not freeform sentences.
An identifier shared by every log line belonging to one request's journey.
A numeric measurement over time - request counts, error rates, durations.
The connected story of one request across handlers, jobs and services.
Service level objective - the measurable reliability promise, like success rate targets.
A condition on metrics that summons a human before users give up.

concepts.name: Logs answer questions, not decorate terminals
concepts.explanation: Write logs for the investigator you will become: who did what, to which resource, with what outcome - as fields. 'Payment webhook rejected: signature invalid, event=evt_123' answers a question; 'error occurred' starts a archaeology dig. Every line carries the correlation id tying it to its request-mates.

concepts.name: Alert on symptoms, diagnose with causes
concepts.explanation: Users feel failed payments and slow pages - alert THERE. CPU spikes and disk noise are causes worth investigating, not paging people about. An SLO makes this concrete: state the target ('at least 99 percent of requests succeed over a rolling window'), then alert when burn threatens it. Everything else goes to dashboards, not phones.

explanations.title: Three pillars, pragmatically
explanations.body: Logs: the forensic record - structured, correlated, secret-free (Level 2's rules stand). Metrics: cheap numbers aggregated per endpoint - count, error count, duration summary - exposed on a metrics endpoint or simple stats page. Traces: correlation ids propagated from HTTP handler into queue jobs and outbound calls connect the whole journey. You do not need purchased platforms to learn these; you need the habits.

explanations.title: The incident drill
explanations.body: Observability untested is decoration. Inject a realistic failure into your own app - a dependency timeout, a webhook rejection storm - then use ONLY your logs, metrics and alerts to detect, bound and diagnose it. Time the detection. Note what you could NOT answer; those gaps are next sprint's instrumentation backlog.

examples.title: The 3am question
examples.description: 'Did payment webhooks fail overnight?' Structured logs answer in seconds: filter event-type equals webhook, outcome equals rejected, last twelve hours - count, event ids, reasons. Freeform log files answer the same question with grep and prayers.

examples.title: Following one request across worlds
examples.description: User submits an expense; handler logs start with correlation id c-881; enqueue job logs carry the same id; worker completion carries it too. One search reveals the entire biography - request to consequence - which is precisely what you want during an incident.

commonMistakes.mistake: Logging everything at maximum verbosity 'to be safe', drowning signal in noise.
commonMistakes.fix: Log decisions, transitions and failures with intent. Volume without purpose hides the smoking gun inside haystacks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Alerting on internal causes - CPU, memory, restart counts - instead of user-facing symptoms.
commonMistakes.fix: Anchor alerts to SLOs users would feel breaching. Causes feed investigation after the page, not the page itself.

agentGuidance: Commission a logging schema BEFORE more code ships: field names, types, forbidden contents (payloads, secrets), correlation-id propagation points. Then have your agent wire every route and job through it uniformly. Ask for the metrics endpoint listing per-route counts/errors/durations - and a README section mapping each metric to the question it answers.

project.title: Watchtower
project.brief: Build the Ledger's nervous system: structured correlated logging across requests AND background jobs, a metrics endpoint exposing per-route health, a written SLO with an alert rule, and a timed incident drill using nothing but your own instrumentation.
requirements: All routes and workers emit structured JSON logs carrying a shared correlation id per request-job chain
Metrics endpoint exposes per-route request count, error count and duration summary - plus job outcomes
SLO statement written: the reliability promise for this app, with the metric that measures it

Grep-audit proves zero payload/secret contents in logs

functional: Correlation id connects a request's log lines through to its spawned jobs - demonstrated end to end
Metrics endpoint reports accurate per-route counts, errors and durations after scripted traffic

architecture: One logging module owns schema and propagation - zero ad-hoc console lines in routes

verificationPrompt: Stress-test my Watchtower instrumentation as the on-call engineer during a simulated night incident - judge only what the system tells you, not what you can read from my code. I will trigger a hidden failure; use ONLY logs and metrics to: (1) detect that something is wrong and note how long detection took, (2) bound the blast radius - which routes and jobs are affected, (3) identify the failing component and current status, (4) decide the first mitigation action. Then grade PASS or FAIL each DoD item and list every question you COULD NOT answer with my observability - that list is my backlog.
reviewQuestions: State your SLO and name the exact metric watching it.
Trace one request's correlation id across handler, job and response.
During the drill, what could your tools NOT tell you - and what will you add first?

Practice incidents calmly before production runs them for real

title: CI/CD Pipelines
summary: Automating build-test-deploy: artifacts built once, environments promoted, gates that never forget.
objective: Automate the road from commit to production: a pipeline running quality gates on every push, building ONE artifact promoted across environments, deployment gates that block bad releases, and secrets handled correctly.

vocabulary.meaning: The automated sequence from code change to deployed software.
The built, versioned output of one pipeline run - what actually deploys.
A pre-production environment configured like production for final verification.
Moving the SAME artifact forward: staging, then production.
An automated check that must pass before deployment continues.

concepts.name: Build once, promote everywhere
concepts.explanation: The artifact that passed staging IS the artifact production receives. Rebuilding per environment means deploying something nobody tested - configuration drift wearing a lab coat. Environment differences belong in environment variables injected at deploy time, not recompiled into new binaries.

concepts.name: Gates outperform memory
concepts.explanation: Humans forget to run tests under deadline pressure; pipelines never do. Typecheck, tests, curriculum validation, build - automated on every push, blocking merges when red. The gate converts your team's standards from documentation into physics.

explanations.title: Pipeline anatomy
explanations.body: Push triggers the pipeline: install dependencies from lockfile, lint and typecheck, run the test suite, validate curriculum data, build the artifact once. Green artifact deploys to staging automatically; promotion to production follows the same artifact after gates pass. Secrets enter the pipeline through the CI platform's encrypted settings - referenced by name in workflow files, values never present in code.

explanations.title: Fast feedback is a feature
explanations.body: A pipeline taking hours teaches people to stop waiting. Keep the main gate fast enough to run on every push: fail on the first broken stage, parallelize independent stages, keep suites lean. Slow pipelines get bypassed psychologically long before anyone dares bypass them technically.

examples.title: Red means stop
examples.description: A commit breaks one test. Pipeline flags red; merge blocked; deploy never runs. The bug died in CI instead of in front of users - which is the entire business case for the twenty minutes spent writing the workflow file.

examples.title: Preview deployments
examples.description: Many platforms spin a temporary live URL per branch or pull request. Reviewers click reality instead of imagining it. Your curriculum site can demo every change before it lands on main - gates plus previews make review concrete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing secrets into workflow files or build scripts because 'CI needed the key'.
commonMistakes.fix: Secrets go in the CI platform's encrypted variable store, referenced by name. Workflow files stay committable and clean - audit them like code because they ARE code with production power.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating flaky red builds as normal, rerunning until green.
commonMistakes.fix: A flaky gate trains everyone to ignore the gate. Fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately - a red everyone ignores is worse than no gate.

agentGuidance: Have your agent author the pipeline definition, then EXPLAIN every stage: what it installs, what command runs, what blocks progression. You review the explanation before merging - pipeline files are production code with deploy powers, deserving the same review rigor as authentication changes.

project.title: Pipeline Gate
project.brief: Build the Ledger's automated railway: every push runs install, typecheck, tests and build; one artifact flows to staging-like preview with green-gate promotion to production; secrets stay platform-managed - and you deliberately break a test to watch the gate save you.
requirements: Every push triggers: lockfile-faithful install, lint/typecheck, full test suite, build
Single artifact built per run and deployed onward - staging and production serve the same artifact
Production promotion gated on green stages - red pipeline physically cannot reach production
Secrets referenced by name from CI platform settings; zero secret values in repo files
Deliberate break: sabotage a test, capture the blocked merge/deploy evidence, restore green
Workflow file reviewed line by line with your agent explaining each stage's purpose
project.agentContext: Create a CI/CD pipeline for my Expense Ledger on my git host's CI platform. Stages: install from lockfile, lint + typecheck, test suite, build artifact once. Artifact auto-deploys to a staging/preview environment; production promotion uses the same artifact and requires green stages. Secrets referenced by encrypted platform variables only. Walk me through the finished workflow file line by line - I approve understanding, not just existence. Then coach my deliberate-break exercise: sabotage, observe the block, document, restore.

functional: Green push produces artifact and staging deployment automatically - links/evidence captured
Sabotaged test blocked merge/deploy - evidence archived, then restored to green
Production received the same artifact staging verified - provenance documented
architecture: Environment differences flow through env vars at deploy time - single artifact serves both environments
Pipeline definition lives in the repo and reads like documentation
security: Zero secret values in repository files - names referenced from platform's encrypted store
Workflow audited for injection risks: untrusted input never interpolated into shell commands
testing: Break-exercise evidence archived: red gate visibly prevented deploy
Full push-to-staging round trip executed and timed
production: README documents pipeline stages, required secret NAMES, and promotion flow

verificationPrompt: Audit my Pipeline Gate as a release engineer reviewing someone's deploy automation for the first time. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) trace one commit through every stage - did each gate genuinely run, or skip quietly?, (2) confirm the artifact reaching production is the one staging verified - how is provenance visible?, (3) attempt to argue a bypass: which shortcut would a rushed teammate take, and does the pipeline prevent it?, (4) inspect the workflow file for secret exposure and shell-injection risks from untrusted input. Finish with the two weakest links in my pipeline and the cheapest fix for each.

Where do your pipeline's secrets live, and who can read them?

Handle CI secrets and workflow files with production-code discipline

title: Failure Handling
summary: Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bounded retries and honest degradation when dependencies wobble.
objective: Design for partial failure as the normal case: explicit timeouts on every remote call, retries bounded with backoff, circuit breakers stopping cascade damage, graceful degradation keeping features alive in reduced form - rehearsed with chaos drills.

vocabulary.meaning: The maximum wait you grant a call before giving up and moving on.
Aggressive automatic retries amplifying an outage into a self-inflicted flood.
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency temporarily, letting it recover.
Continuing reduced service - cached data, fewer features - instead of hard failure.
The designed alternative answer used when the primary path is unavailable.

concepts.name: Everything remote eventually fails
concepts.explanation: Networks partition, services restart, providers deploy maintenance windows mid-your-peak. On a long enough timeline every dependency WILL be down while users watch. Systems assuming otherwise do not avoid failure - they just meet it unrehearsed. The professional posture: partial failure is Tuesday, design for it.

concepts.name: Fail smaller, not harder
concepts.explanation: One dead dependency should cost you one degraded feature - not a hung server, not cascading collapse. Isolation comes from three boring tools applied everywhere: explicit timeouts (no call hangs forever), bounded retries with backoff (no storm amplification), and circuit breakers (stop feeding a failing dependency requests it cannot answer).

explanations.title: Timeouts are love letters to your future self
explanations.body: Every outbound call - HTTP fetch, database query, queue operation - carries an explicit maximum wait sized honestly for the operation. Without one, a stalled dependency holds your threads hostage while requests pile up: your outage is now THEIR outage, multiplied. With timeouts, failure arrives fast, small and diagnosable instead of slow, total and mysterious.

explanations.title: Breakers and degradation ladders
explanations.body: Circuit breaker logic: after consecutive failures cross a threshold, STOP calling - trip open. Requests during the open window receive the fallback instantly. Periodically allow one probe through (half-open); success closes the circuit again. Meanwhile features degrade along a designed ladder: fresh data, then cached data flagged 'as of when', then static default, then an honest error. Each rung is chosen in calm daylight, never invented at midnight.

examples.title: Currency rates, degraded gracefully
examples.description: Ledger shows expenses converted to your currency using an external rates API. API dies? Breaker trips within seconds; UI switches to yesterday's cached rates labeled 'rates as of yesterday'; conversions remain possible, slightly stale, honestly labeled. Nobody's evening ruined.

examples.title: The retry that made it worse
examples.description: Dependency slows to five-second responses. Naive clients time out at three seconds, retry instantly, doubling load - the struggling service now faces twice the traffic. Bounded retries WITH backoff and jitter refuse to amplify: few attempts, spaced out, capped.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying on default timeouts - or none - because 'it usually responds fast'.
commonMistakes.fix: Every remote call declares its maximum wait explicitly. Usually-fast is not a contract; timeouts are.

commonMistakes.mistake: Unlimited immediate retries 'until it works'.
commonMistakes.fix: Cap attempts, space them with growing delays and jitter. Otherwise your resilience code becomes a DDoS bot loyal to you.

agentGuidance: Demand a dependency inventory: every outbound call listed with its timeout value, retry policy, breaker thresholds and fallback behavior - BEFORE wiring features that use it. Centralize HTTP client defaults so the table is enforced by code, not convention. A dependency without a row in that table is an unaudited risk.

project.title: Storm Doors
project.brief: Harden the Ledger against a wobbling world: add a currency-conversion feature backed by a keyless external rates API, wrapped in explicit timeouts, bounded backoff retries, a visible circuit breaker, stale-cache fallback and a kill switch - then run a chaos drill and document the timeline.
requirements: External rates call carries explicit timeout; no other outbound call lacks one either
Retries bounded: max attempts, exponential-ish backoff with jitter, cap enforced
Circuit breaker trips after consecutive failures, half-open probes recover - state visible in metrics
Degradation ladder implemented: fresh rates, cached rates labeled with age, conversion disabled with honest message
Kill switch env var disables the external feature outright without redeploying code
Chaos drill documented: network cut mid-flow, behavior timeline recorded minute by minute
project.agentContext: Add currency-conversion display to my Expense Ledger backed by a keyless FX-rates API. Wrap it properly: explicit per-call timeout, bounded retries with jittered backoff, circuit breaker whose state shows in my metrics, fallback ladder serving cached rates with visible age labels, kill-switch env var. Build a dependency-inventory table first covering ALL my outbound calls with timeout/retry/fallback columns - fill gaps found elsewhere too. Then coach my chaos drill: I cut the network, we narrate the timeline together.

functional: Healthy path shows converted amounts normally; degraded path shows cached rates with clear age labels
Breaker trips after the agreed failure threshold; half-open recovery restores fresh rates automatically
Kill switch disables the feature completely without code changes
architecture: Dependency inventory table complete: EVERY outbound call has timeout, retry policy, fallback documented
HTTP client defaults centralized - table enforced by shared code
testing: Chaos drill executed: network severed mid-flow; timeline recorded showing graceful degradation steps
Retry budget verified bounded - no unbounded hammering observable in logs

verificationPrompt: Run a hostile resilience review of my Storm Doors - you are the hurricane. Attempt each: (1) sever the rates API entirely - walk my degradation ladder rung by rung and confirm labels stay honest, (2) make responses SLOW rather than dead - did timeouts hold or did requests pile up?, (3) watch my retries during an outage - prove they stayed bounded and did not amplify the incident, (4) force the breaker open then partially heal the dependency - did half-open probing behave as documented? Grade every DoD item, then nominate the dependency most likely to ruin my worst day and whether my doors hold against it.
reviewQuestions: Recite your dependency inventory: who talks to the outside world, and with what timeout?
Why do immediate unlimited retries convert outages into self-inflicted wounds?
Describe your degradation ladder for the currency feature - and who chose each rung.
capabilities: Give every remote call explicit timeouts and bounded retries
Stop cascades with circuit breakers and honest fallbacks
Rehearse partial failure until it is boring

title: Distributed Systems Thinking
summary: Latency, partial failure and consistency tradeoffs as the default condition - not the exception.
objective: Reason about systems spanning multiple processes and machines: why network calls are not function calls, what partial failure means for correctness, and how to choose - and document - consistency and latency tradeoffs deliberately.

vocabulary.meaning: Software running across multiple processes or machines that coordinate over a network.
Some components working while others fail - the state distributed systems live in.
The time an operation takes end to end; across networks it dominates local computation.
The guarantee that all readers see the same data at the same moment.
A break in the network splitting parts of a system from each other.

concepts.name: A network call is not a function call
concepts.explanation: Calling a function in-process either runs or throws. Calling another machine can run, throw, hang, vanish mid-flight after doing the work, or succeed while the reply is lost forever. That extra universe of outcomes - especially 'did it actually happen?' - is the entire subject of distributed systems.

concepts.name: Tradeoffs are chosen, not escaped
concepts.explanation: When a partition strikes, you choose between refusing requests (staying consistent) and serving possibly-stale answers (staying available). Neither is free, and the right choice varies per feature: bank balances lean consistent, product pages lean available. Seniority here is writing down which you chose, where, and why.

explanations.title: The questions every boundary asks
explanations.body: Split any work across two processes and inherit four questions: What if the other side is slow? (timeouts - Level 3). What if the call never arrives? (retries with dedup). What if both sides think they succeeded? (reconciliation). Who is right when they disagree? (a documented decision). Systems that never answered these on paper answer them at 3am by accident.

explanations.title: Start with two, not twenty
explanations.body: You learn distributed thinking by splitting ONE responsibility out of your app - say, report generation becoming its own service reading from the same store - and observing everything that gets harder: deployment, monitoring, failure isolation, version skew between halves. Two services already exhibit nearly every disease of two hundred; the scale changes, the physics does not.

examples.title: The vanishing write
examples.description: Ledger calls the reporting service to log a summary update. The service receives it, writes it, then crashes before responding. Ledger times out and retries. Was the update applied once, twice, or never? Without idempotent handling nobody knows - this exact fog motivates the next modules.

examples.title: Two services, one user question
examples.description: 'Did my expense save?' now has a compound answer: the API committed it, but the search index lags thirty seconds behind. The honest UI says 'saved - indexing shortly'. Distributed literacy is knowing WHICH truth each component holds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Designing as if calls between services behave like local functions.
commonMistakes.fix: For every cross-service call ask: what if it hangs, duplicates, or succeeds invisibly? Write the answer down before coding against it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Debugging cross-service issues without shared correlation ids.
commonMistakes.fix: Propagate request ids across every hop (Level 3's Watchtower habit) BEFORE splitting anything further.

agentGuidance: Before any split, make your agent produce a boundary contract: what crosses the line, what happens on timeout, duplicate delivery, and reorder - plus which consistency choice each read makes. Reviewing that one page prevents entire categories of accidental architecture.

project.title: Split Decision
project.brief: Extract ONE responsibility of the Ledger into a second local service, put a fault-injecting proxy between them, and write the decision memo documenting every tradeoff you chose - then attack your own design with chaos probes.
requirements: One capability extracted into a separate process communicating over HTTP - reports or notifications are natural candidates
Fault-injection proxy between services: configurable latency, dropped responses, duplicate responses
Boundary contract written: endpoints, timeout values, retry policy, duplicate-handling expectations
Consistency decisions documented per feature: what may lag, what must not, and what users see during lag
Chaos session performed: kill the second service mid-request, observe behavior, record findings against the memo
project.agentContext: Help me extract one Ledger capability into a second local service with a fault-injecting proxy between us. Before code: draft the boundary contract together - who calls whom, timeouts, retry rules, duplicate-delivery assumptions, and my consistency choices per feature. Then implement minimally. Then coach my chaos drills: inject latency, drop responses, duplicate them, kill the service mid-call - I record observed behavior against our memo and we patch the gaps honestly.

functional: Both services run locally and complete the full feature flow through the proxy
Chaos drill executed: latency injection, response drops, duplicates, hard kill - behavior recorded for each
System survives second-service death with defined degradation, not a hung first service
architecture: Boundary contract document exists and matches implementation
Correlation ids propagate across the service boundary - traceable in both services' logs
security: Service-to-service traffic carries no secrets beyond what the boundary needs
testing: Memo-vs-reality review completed: every divergence between planned and observed behavior patched or explicitly deferred
production: README carries the decision memo: tradeoffs chosen, alternatives rejected, chaos findings

verificationPrompt: Interrogate my Split Decision like a systems architect auditing a boundary drawn in pencil. Verify PASS or FAIL with evidence: (1) run my chaos drills yourself through the fault proxy - do behaviors match what the memo claims?, (2) find the undefined case: name ONE failure mode my boundary contract does not cover, (3) check correlation ids actually cross the boundary in logs, (4) challenge my consistency choices: pick one feature and argue the opposite tradeoff. Finish by grading the memo itself - would you let a team ship based on it?
reviewQuestions: Which outcomes differ between calling a function and calling another machine?
State one consistency-versus-availability decision YOU made, and its cost when wrong.
What did killing the second service reveal that happy-path testing never could?
capabilities: Reason about latency, duplication and partial failure at boundaries
Write boundary contracts and consistency decisions down
Chaos-test designs before production does it for free

title: Event-Driven Architecture
summary: Producers announcing facts, consumers reacting independently - events instead of synchronous chains.
objective: Replace synchronous call chains with published domain events: producers emit facts once, independent consumers react at their own pace, failures isolate per consumer - governed by explicit event schemas.

vocabulary.meaning: A recorded fact that something happened, e.g. expense.created - past tense, immutable.
The component that publishes events when facts occur.
A component subscribed to event types and reacting to them.
Infrastructure storing and delivering events between producers and consumers.
The declared shape and versioning rules of an event's payload.

concepts.name: Announce, do not ask
concepts.explanation: Synchronous design: creating an expense directly calls the notifier, the reporter, the auditor - coupling their fates together. Event-driven design: the creator announces expense.created ONCE and moves on; interested parties subscribe and react independently. Slow or broken consumers no longer hold up creation - the defining win.

concepts.name: Events are immutable history
concepts.explanation: An event records that something HAPPENED - it does not get edited, only superseded by new events. Consumers evolve independently because the fact stays true even as interpretations multiply. Schema discipline keeps this honest: additive changes with new fields, never silent rewrites of meaning.

explanations.title: From choreography to contracts
explanations.body: Each consumer owns its reaction to an event type; the producer neither knows nor cares who listens. The discipline keeping this sane is the schema: event name, fields, types, version. Adding optional fields is safe evolution; removing or repurposing fields breaks every consumer quietly. Treat schemas like API contracts because they ARE one - just asynchronous.

explanations.title: Failure isolation and the fine print
explanations.body: Five consumers listening means five independent failure domains: the notifier crashing never blocks the reporter. The fine print: deliveries are at-least-once (consumers need dedupe awareness), ordering guarantees vary by infrastructure, and a dead broker stops EVERYTHING - which is why broker health joins your observability board the day events go live.

examples.title: Two consumers, zero coupling
examples.description: expense.created publishes; the audit-log consumer appends a line while the digest-builder updates aggregates. Add a fraud-detector next month: subscribe it, touch nothing else. The producer's code never changed - that is the decoupling paying off.

examples.title: Schema drift horror story
examples.description: Someone renames amount to value in an event without versioning. One consumer silently reads undefined for weeks, corrupting totals. The fix is boring and absolute: versions on schemas, additive-only changes within a version, consumers validating what they receive.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chaining events secretly - consumer B publishing C triggering D - until nothing can be traced.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep flows visible: a written map of which event triggers which consumers. Hidden orchestration is undebuggable orchestration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating event meaning in place - same name, different payload semantics.
commonMistakes.fix: Version events explicitly; new shape earns a new version. Consumers migrate on their own schedule.

agentGuidance: Insist on an event catalog before wiring: event names in past tense, schema per event with version, producer, current subscribers, delivery guarantees assumed. When your agent proposes a new event, the catalog entry comes FIRST - code follows contracts here more than anywhere else.

project.title: Event Wire
project.brief: Wire the Ledger for events: domain events publish from core writes through a local broker, two independent consumers react (audit trail, digest builder), consumer failures isolate cleanly - all governed by versioned schemas and a visible event catalog.
requirements: Core writes publish domain events (at minimum: created, updated, deleted) through one broker abstraction
Two independent consumers: audit-log appender and weekly-digest builder - each owning its failures
Killing one consumer never blocks the producer or the other consumer - demonstrated live
Versioned event schemas documented in a catalog; payloads validated on consume
Duplicate delivery handled: replaying an event produces no duplicated side effects
Broker restart-safe: unpublished/pending events survive process death
project.agentContext: Add event-driven architecture to my Expense Ledger. Start with the event catalog: names in past tense, versioned schemas, producers and subscribers listed. Use a boring durable local broker (database-backed is fine) behind one publish/subscribe interface. Implement audit-log and weekly-digest consumers as fully isolated processes. Prove failure isolation by killing one consumer mid-stream, prove duplicate safety by replaying events, and persist pending events across restarts. Show me the catalog before any wiring.

functional: Writing an expense publishes events consumed by BOTH consumers independently
Consumer killed mid-stream: producer unaffected, other consumer unaffected, recovery clean
Replayed/duplicated event causes no duplicated side effects in either consumer
Pending events survive broker/process restart - nothing silently lost
architecture: Event catalog matches implementation exactly - every wired event documented with version
Consumers validate incoming payloads against schemas before acting
security: Event payloads carry ids and minimal fields, not full sensitive documents
testing: Isolation test: stop consumer A, verify consumer B still processes while A's events queue up
Replay test: duplicate deliveries asserted harmless
production: README carries the event catalog and the consumer-failure runbook

verificationPrompt: Chaos-audit my Event Wire as a skeptical platform engineer who has been burned by hidden couplings. Attempt each probe and report results: (1) kill the audit consumer mid-stream - does the digest builder keep flowing and events queue for the dead one?, (2) replay the same event ten times - any duplicated side effects anywhere?, (3) deliver events slightly out of order - what breaks, honestly?, (4) diff my event catalog against actual wire traffic - any undocumented event or field? Grade each DoD item, then tell me which consumer would rot first in production and what early-warning signal I am missing.
reviewQuestions: Contrast asking services directly versus announcing facts - what changed in your code?
Why must event schemas version instead of mutating?
Where did duplicate delivery try to bite you, and what absorbed it?
capabilities: Decouple features with published events and independent consumers
Govern event shapes with versioned schemas
Isolate consumer failures so one sink never drags down the flow

title: Idempotency and Retries
summary: Operations safe to repeat: idempotency keys, dedup windows and retry budgets that respect both sides.
objective: Make unsafe operations repeatable by design: client-supplied idempotency keys with stored responses, dedupe windows, concurrent-submit handling - plus retry policies with budgets so clients back off politely instead of stampeding.

vocabulary.meaning: One whose repetition after the first call leaves no additional effect.
A caller-provided unique marker letting the server recognize and absorb repeats.
How long the server remembers processed keys before forgetting them.
A cap on total retry traffic so clients cannot amplify incidents.
Delivery guarantee promising attempts happen - possibly more than once.

concepts.name: Retries turn blips into successes - or bugs into disasters
concepts.explanation: A timeout followed by a successful retry rescues ordinary network weather. But if the FIRST attempt actually landed server-side, the blind retry now double-charges, double-books or double-sends. Idempotency keys convert dangerous retries into safe ones: same key, same stored result - the operation addresses itself.

concepts.name: Exactly-once is really at-least-once plus dedupe
concepts.explanation: No practical system guarantees exactly-once execution by magic; they guarantee at-least-once ATTEMPTS and give you the tools to make effects once-only: keys, stored responses, dedupe windows. Understanding this reframes every 'guaranteed exactly-once' claim you will ever read.

explanations.title: The key lifecycle
explanations.body: Client generates a unique key per logical operation (uuid works) and sends it on the request. Server checks: seen this key recently? Return the STORED original response without re-executing. Otherwise execute, store key-plus-response inside the same transaction as the effect, set expiry. The subtle part is concurrency: two identical requests racing must resolve to one execution - via unique constraints or locks - never two.

explanations.title: Retry etiquette
explanations.body: Clients owe the server restraint: bounded attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After headers, and a total budget so a misbehaving loop cannot multiply load indefinitely. Servers owe callers clarity: 409-style signals for conflicts, idempotency support on every unsafe endpoint. Politeness on both sides is what keeps partial failure from becoming total failure.

examples.title: Double-click, single charge
examples.description: User double-clicks Pay; both requests carry the same idempotency key. First executes and stores its response under the key. Second finds the stored response and returns it verbatim - one charge, two identical replies, calm user. Without the key: two charges, one furious support ticket.

examples.title: The crash between accept and apply
examples.description: Server accepts a transfer, crashes before committing. Client retried with the SAME key: the half-finished attempt left nothing stored, so the retry executes cleanly. Different key would have risked a second transfer - key discipline is the whole ballgame.

commonMistakes.mistake: Generating a fresh key per RETRY instead of per OPERATION.
commonMistakes.fix: Key lives across the operation's retries - regenerate only for genuinely new operations. Per-retry keys are theater.

commonMistakes.mistake: Remembering keys forever, or worse, for seconds only.
commonMistakes.fix: Choose a dedupe window honestly from retry horizons - long enough to cover realistic retries, short enough to bound storage. Document it.

agentGuidance: Specify the contract before code: which endpoints accept keys, header name, window length, concurrent-race strategy, and the exact stored-response replay format. Ask your agent to write the race-condition test FIRST - two parallel same-key requests - because concurrency is precisely where hand-rolled dedupe falls apart.

project.title: Replay Shield
project.brief: Armor the Ledger's unsafe endpoints with real idempotency: key-based request dedupe storing original responses, race-proof against parallel submits, TTL'd windows - and a documented client retry policy your own scripts obey.
requirements: Unsafe endpoints (create/update/delete/payment-flavored) accept an idempotency-key header
First request executes and stores key plus response; replays return the STORED response with a replay marker
Concurrent identical-key requests resolve to exactly one execution - race-tested
Dedupe entries expire after a documented window; expired keys re-execute honestly
Client retry policy documented: max attempts, backoff curve, Retry-After obedience, total budget
Your own test scripts demonstrate compliance with that policy
project.agentContext: Implement idempotency for my Expense Ledger's unsafe endpoints. Contract first: header name, window TTL, storage schema (key, request fingerprint, response, status, expiry), and the concurrency strategy for two same-key requests racing - propose options. Stored responses replay verbatim with an idempotency-replayed marker header. Write the parallel-submission race test BEFORE implementation, watch it fail, then build until green including it. Finally draft the client retry policy and a script that obeys it.

functional: Repeat request with same key returns stored original response - marked as replay - with no new side effects
Parallel identical requests produce exactly one execution and matching responses
Different keys to the same logical operation DO execute separately (key is doing the work)
Expired-window key re-executes rather than serving ancient cached responses
architecture: Idempotency enforced in one middleware layer, declared per-route - not copy-pasted into handlers
Key storage rides in the same transaction story as effects - no orphan executions possible
security: Keys scoped per account: user A cannot read or poison user B's stored responses by guessing keys
Stored responses leak nothing across accounts even when payloads overlap
testing: Race test green: concurrent same-key storm resolves to single execution
Crash-window test: simulated failure after accept still allows clean same-key retry
production: README documents the idempotency contract and client retry policy

verificationPrompt: Attack my Replay Shield as a hostile client who profits from double-execution. Attempt each and grade PASS or FAIL against my DoD: (1) fire fifty parallel requests sharing one key - count actual executions; anything above one is blood, (2) reuse ANOTHER USER's key verbatim - did you see their stored response or influence their execution?, (3) wait out the dedupe window and replay - does it behave exactly as documented?, (4) hammer retries WITHOUT backoff - does my retry-budget documentation describe behavior my server actually enforces? Then identify which endpoint still lacks shield coverage and what one request there could double-execute today.
reviewQuestions: Explain why exactly-once is marketed but at-least-once-plus-dedupe is engineered.
Walk through your key lifecycle: generation, storage, replay, expiry.
What does your client owe your server during an outage - and vice versa?
capabilities: Design unsafe operations to be repeat-safe via keys and stored responses
Handle concurrent duplicate submissions race-free
Set retry etiquette that survives contact with real outages

title: Eventual Consistency
summary: Read-after-write gaps, conflicts and multi-step workflows - designing UX and undo paths for stale truth.
objective: Design workflows that span multiple reliable steps: handle read-after-write gaps honestly, resolve concurrent-update conflicts deliberately, and build saga-style sequences where every step has a compensating partner.

vocabulary.meaning: A model where replicas converge over time - reads may briefly disagree with writes.
The window where a fresh write is not yet visible to subsequent reads.
Two writers updating the same data concurrently, requiring a resolution rule.
A multi-step workflow where each step pairs with a compensation for rollback.
The semantic undo of a completed step - refund the charge, release the booking.

concepts.name: Stale reads are normal - design the UX for them
concepts.explanation: In distributed stores, the write you just made may not appear on the next read for a moment. Fighting this with denial produces bug reports; embracing it produces design: optimistic interfaces showing pending states, read-your-own-writes routing for the author, and labels admitting freshness honestly. The lie 'always instantly consistent everywhere' is unavailable at any price once you scale.

concepts.name: Every step needs its undo
concepts.explanation: Classic transactions span one database; real workflows span many services and cannot share one commit button. Sagas replace atomicity with choreography: each step commits locally and declares its compensating action - charge pairs with refund, reservation pairs with release. Failure mid-sequence triggers compensations in reverse, returning the world to honesty.

explanations.title: Living with the gap
explanations.body: Three practical tools. Route the author's next read to wherever their write landed (read-your-writes). Show pending/syncing states in UI instead of pretending instant truth. Timestamp displayed data so staleness is visible ('updated 30s ago'). None require exotic infrastructure - they require deciding, per feature, how much staleness users can feel and forgive.

explanations.title: Conflicts and compensations
explanations.body: Concurrent edits need a rule chosen in daylight: last-write-wins loses data quietly; version checks reject stale overwrites loudly; field-level merges preserve most intent. For multi-step flows, design the saga BEFORE shipping: enumerate steps, pair each with compensation, decide what happens when a compensation ITSELF fails - that escalation path goes to humans, visibly.

examples.title: The disappearing comment
examples.description: User posts a comment; the list refreshes from a lagging replica and shows nothing. Support ticket filed: 'your app ate my comment'. With a pending-state design, the same user sees their comment marked 'syncing' - truth arrives late but arrives visibly, trust intact.

examples.title: Booking trip, hotel fails
examples.description: Saga steps: book flight (committed), book hotel (fails). Compensation fires: cancel flight automatically, notify user honestly. No step pretends atomicity existed; the workflow's job is making the eventual state CORRECT even when intermediate states were messy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming read-after-write everywhere because the demo worked on one node.
commonMistakes.fix: Identify which reads are author-sensitive and route/label them accordingly. Test on two replicas with real lag, not in imagination.

commonMistakes.mistake: Multi-step workflows without designed compensations - 'we'll add undo later'.
commonMistakes.fix: No step ships without its named undo. If a step cannot be compensated, it must be idempotent-and-retryable or human-approved - decide explicitly.

Have your agent generate failure-injection tests for EVERY step boundary - between-step crashes are where orphaned states breed. title: Replication and Sharding
summary: Replicas for reads and survival, shards for writes and size - what each solves and what each breaks.
objective: Understand and rehearse data-scaling's two levers: replication spreading reads and surviving machine loss, sharding spreading writes and datasets - including replica-lag reality, shard-key consequences, and the honesty to know when neither is needed yet.

vocabulary.meaning: Keeping copies of the same data on multiple nodes.
The delay before copies reflect the primary's latest writes.
Splitting DIFFERENT rows across nodes so no single machine holds everything.
The column deciding which shard owns each row - effectively choosing your future queries.
A shard receiving disproportionate load because its key range got popular.

concepts.name: Replicas spread reads; shards spread rows
concepts.explanation: Replication copies the WHOLE dataset onto additional machines: read throughput scales, and losing one machine loses nothing permanent. Sharding splits the dataset so DIFFERENT machines own DIFFERENT rows: write throughput and dataset size scale beyond any single box. Most applications need the first far earlier than the second.

concepts.name: The shard key chooses your queries' fate
concepts.explanation: Shard by tenant_id and tenant-scoped queries fly while cross-tenant analytics scatter-gather painfully. Shard by date and recent data burns hot while archives idle. Resharding later is major surgery - so the key decision is less about today's speed than about which tomorrows remain possible. Choose like it is permanent, because practically it is.

explanations.title: Lag is the tax on copies
explanations.body: Primary accepts writes; replicas catch up continuously but never instantly. Read-from-replica architectures buy throughput by selling freshness: dashboards may trail seconds behind. The classic self-inflicted wound: write then immediately read from a lagging replica and swear the write vanished. Cure: route author-following reads to the primary briefly - read-your-writes - and label everything else's freshness honestly.

explanations.title: Sharding is surgery; avoid until proven necessary
explanations.body: Shards complicate transactions, joins, backups, rebalancing and every query that crosses boundaries. Honest sequence: indexes first (Level 3), caching second, read replicas third, THEN shards when write volume or dataset size demonstrably demands it. Teams that shard early ship slower and debug longer; teams that shard when justified can - because they learned the rest first.

examples.title: Reports move to the replica
examples.description: Month-end aggregations hammered the primary until heavy reads moved to a replica. Dashboards now trail by a few labeled seconds; transactional paths breathe easy. Total cost: one routing config change and one freshness label.

examples.title: Tenant-bound sharding
examples.description: A multi-team ledger shards by workspace id: every team's rows live together, team queries hit exactly one shard, and cross-team reports are acknowledged as batch jobs - designed around, not apologized for. The key choice made every OTHER decision simple.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading your own writes from a lagging replica and filing 'data loss' bugs.
commonMistakes.fix: Read-your-writes routing for immediate follow-ups; explicit freshness labeling elsewhere. Teach the UX to expect the gap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a shard key from today's query patterns without modeling tomorrow's.
commonMistakes.fix: Document the key analysis: which queries stay single-shard, which scatter, what volume shifts break it. Permanent decisions deserve memos.

agentGuidance: Demand lag visibility before routing ANY reads elsewhere: measure replication delay, expose it, alert on growth. When evaluating shard keys, make your agent simulate query distributions against candidate keys - show me the single-shard versus scatter ratio for each candidate before I choose.

title: Load Balancing and Horizontal Scaling
summary: Stateless services behind balancers, sessions in shared stores, autoscaling driven by honest signals.
objective: Run multiple interchangeable instances behind a load balancer: eliminate singleton state, steer traffic with health checks, survive instance death without user impact, and draft an autoscaling policy anchored to symptoms users feel.

vocabulary.meaning: Traffic director distributing requests across healthy instances.
Adding more machines instead of enlarging one - capacity by count.
An instance holding nothing unique - any replica can serve any request.
The balancer's probe deciding whether an instance deserves traffic.
Pinning one user to one instance - usually a smell indicating hidden state.

concepts.name: Any instance can die at any moment
concepts.explanation: Horizontal scaling's premise: instances are livestock, not pets. That premise holds ONLY when no instance owns anything unique - no memory-resident sessions, no local file uploads, no in-process rate counters. Statelessness is not an architecture diagram; it is the property that lets a balancer drop one of five instances mid-rush and users never notice.

concepts.name: Autoscale on symptoms, stabilize with cooldowns
concepts.explanation: Scaling triggers belong on user-feel signals - request latency, queue depth - not vanity CPU graphs that spike during harmless bursts. Add cooldown periods so the fleet breathes instead of flapping up-down-up-down, and remember scale-IN kills instances too: graceful drain before death, or you shed users mid-request.

explanations.title: The statelessness audit
explanations.body: Every piece of in-memory state is a scaling landmine: sessions (move to shared store - Level 2 already did), rate-limit counters (shared - Level 3 did), cache (shared or per-instance-with-TTL tolerance), uploaded files (object storage, not local disk). Run the audit honestly: restart an instance and inventory what users lose. Whatever appears on that list is tomorrow's refactor ticket.

explanations.title: Balancers and health truths
explanations.body: Health checks decide traffic: a deep check verifying dependencies beats a shallow ping that happily routes to zombie instances. Draining matters equally - when instances leave the pool (deploy or scale-in), in-flight requests finish gracefully rather than dying mid-response. These mechanics decide whether deploys feel invisible or violent.

examples.title: Kill one of two
examples.description: Ledger runs twice behind a local balancer; scripted traffic flows. Kill instance A mid-run: requests in flight drain, new ones route to B, users scroll on unaware. Sessions lived in the shared store, counters were shared - statelessness paid its dividend in a single afternoon demo.

examples.title: The sticky-session trap
examples.description: A team 'fixes' login glitches by enabling sticky sessions. Now instances own users, balancers lose flexibility, one hot instance melts while four idle, and every deploy drops logged-in users. Stickiness was the symptom; un-migrated session state was the disease.

commonMistakes.mistake: Per-instance in-memory caches or counters assumed global after scaling to two.
commonMistakes.fix: Shared store for correctness-critical state (counters); TTL-tolerant treatment for cacheable state. The L3 lessons generalize: anything 'in-process' is now 'per-instance'.

commonMistakes.mistake: Autoscaling on CPU alone, flapping the fleet during spiky traffic.
commonMistakes.fix: Symptom-based triggers plus cooldowns. Scaling that whiplash sheds more capacity than it adds.

agentGuidance: Before adding instance number two, commission the statelessness audit from your agent: list every in-memory assumption (sessions, counters, caches, temp files) and its migration target. Then have health checks assert DEPENDENCY health, not just liveness - a deep check is the difference between balancing and roulette.

title: Fault Tolerance and Disaster Recovery
summary: RTO/RPO targets, backups you have actually restored, and failover rehearsed until boring.
objective: Close the level by planning for bad days: choose RTO/RPO targets honestly, automate encrypted offsite backups with retention, rehearse full restores and primary-loss failover, and hand your runbook to a stranger to execute blind.

vocabulary.meaning: Recovery time objective - maximum tolerable minutes from disaster to restored service.
Recovery point objective - maximum tolerable data loss measured in time.
How many generations of backups are kept, and for how long.
Switching service to a standby when the primary dies.
Actually restoring a backup somewhere real and verifying it - regularly.

concepts.name: An unrestored backup is a rumor
concepts.explanation: Backups earn zero trust until one has been restored, end to end, and the restored system verified against counts and checksums. Corruption propagates too - restoring yesterday's corrupted dump restores the corruption. Hence: automated encrypted backups, offsite copies, tested retention windows, and restore drills scheduled like payroll.

concepts.name: Targets are chosen, then rehearsed
concepts.explanation: RTO and RPO are business decisions wearing engineering clothes: how much data may we lose (RPO sets backup frequency), how long may we stay down (RTO sets failover machinery). Choosing them costs nothing; MEETING them costs automation and rehearsals. The gap between the two is where disasters live.

explanations.title: Backup architecture worth having
explanations.body: Automated on a schedule, encrypted at rest, copied OFFSITE (different region/provider - a backup on the same machine as the data shares its disasters), retention tiered (recent dailies, older weeklies/monthlies), and restoration REHEARSED: pull a random backup, restore to a clean environment, verify row counts and spot-check integrity, time the whole thing. That timing IS your real RTO estimate.

explanations.title: Failure domains and the rehearsal habit
explanations.body: Assume one domain disappears completely - a region, a provider, a disk array. Tolerance means: state replicated or restorable OUTSIDE that domain, DNS/routing able to point somewhere else, and humans who have DONE it before under pressure. Rehearsal converts disaster from improvisation theater into a checklist you have run quarterly.

examples.title: The restore that saved Tuesday
examples.description: Bad migration corrupts the expenses table Friday night. Restore drill muscle memory kicks in: latest verified nightly pulled, restored to standby in the practiced sequence, counts verified, DNS flipped. Users missed an hour; the team missed none of their practice. The drill WAS the disaster plan.

examples.title: Same-shelf backups fail together
examples.description: A startup backed up diligently - onto an external drive sitting beside the server. The office flood took both. Offsite is not paranoia; it is the difference between an outage story and a company-ending one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Backups landing on the same disk, machine or region as the data they protect.
commonMistakes.fix: Offsite, different provider or region, encrypted. A backup sharing fate with its data is decoration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Retention configured once and forgotten until the one backup you need expired.
commonMistakes.fix: Tiered retention reviewed periodically; restore drills PULL FROM REAL ARCHIVE GENERATIONS, not just last night's copy.

agentGuidance: Have your agent script the ENTIRE lifecycle: backup job, encryption, offsite copy, verification checksums, and a restore runbook written for a tired stranger at 3am. Then demand adversarial review OF THE RUNBOOK - your agent should try to execute it finding every ambiguity, because ambiguity at 3am becomes downtime.

Tiered retention configured and DOCUMENTED: dailies, weeklies, monthlies with lifetimes
Restore runbook written for an operator with zero context - every command, every verification step
Full restore DRILL executed to a clean environment: counts/checksums verified, wall-clock time recorded as your real RTO evidence
Primary-loss failover rehearsed: promote standby (or documented equivalent), redirect, verify, fall back
RTO/RPO targets stated upfront; drill results compared against them honestly - gaps listed
